name: Urðarbrunnr
material: Sacred spring beneath a root of Yggdrasil
powers: The well of fate from which the Norns shape the destinies of all beings.
description: Urðarbrunnr, the well of fate that lies beneath the root of the world tree Yggdrasil, beside which the three Norns dwell and shape the fates of men. The gods hold their council there, and swans swim in the well. Each day the Norns water the tree with its clay-white water and dew so that it never withers, making the well the source of all destiny in Norse myth.

name: Witch Broom
material: Birch twigs bound to a handle
powers: Carries the rider to the witches' sabbath mountain Blåkulla.
description: The broom (kvast) that, in Swedish folk belief, carried witches to Blåkulla, the witches' sabbath mountain, especially on Maundy Thursday before Easter. The 'påskkärring', the Easter witch, was thought to ride a broom, or a cow, goat, or pitchfork, to Blåkulla. People blocked chimneys and hid brooms behind stoves to stop the flights, and the belief shaped Sweden's Easter-witch custom.
source: Swedish belief in the Easter witches of Blåkulla

name: The Black Book (Sortebog)
powers: Used by cunning folk to heal the sick, find stolen goods, and undo witchcraft.
description: A handwritten book of prayers, charms, and remedies kept by Danish cunning folk, the 'black book' or Cyprianus, named after the apocryphal magician-bishop Cyprianus of Antioch. The books mixed church prayers with healing formulas against disease, worms, and bewitchment. Hundreds survive in Danish archives as evidence of a living folk magic that continued well into the 19th century.

name: The War Shield of Neith
powers: Emblem of the goddess of war and of weaving.
description: The emblem of the goddess Neith of Sais: a shield across which two crossed arrows are set, combining her natures as a war goddess and a weaver. The symbol is attested as her sign from early Egyptian writing, painted on her temple walls and on votive objects, and the classical authors Plutarch and Herodotus described it. It is one of the oldest goddess emblems of Egypt.
source: Neith emblem on early votives; Plutarch, De Iside

name: The Wesekh Collar
powers: Bestowed solar protection and divine favor on its wearer.
description: The broad beaded collar worn across the chest by pharaohs, queens, and gods, built of rows of faience and semiprecious beads capped by golden falcon-headed terminals. Such collars were given as royal gifts and buried with the dead, who are shown receiving them from deities; Tutankhamun's burial yielded dozens in gold, glass, and stone. The wesekh lent its wearer solar protection and divine favor.

name: The Whistling Arrow
powers: Signal whistle that directed cavalry maneuvers
description: The signal arrow of the Mongol armies, tipped with a drilled bone head that shrieked in flight, used by Genghis Khan's cavalry to direct charges and ambushes across the steppe. Described by Persian and Chinese chroniclers, the whistling arrow survives as a motif of the swift, coordinated warfare that built the empire.
source: Persian and Chinese chronicles of the Mongol campaigns
